extracted.intended_audience: students and technicians working in bacteriological laboratories; laboratory staff responsible for cleaning and sterilisation of glassware and apparatus
extracted.subtask_description: Practical procedures and standards for cleaning, disinfecting, and sterilising glassware, pipettes, slides, cover-slips, and instruments in a bacteriological laboratory, including choice of agents, temperatures, times, and apparatus-use steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning new test-tubes
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the tubes in a bucket or other convenient receptacle, fill with water and add a handful of 'Sapon' or other soap powder; boil for thirty minutes (or autoclave for similar period); cleanse interior with test-tube brushes, rinse thoroughly in cold water; invert to drain; dry and polish inside and out with a soft cloth such as selvyt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule applies as forcibly to new as to old apparatus. Ensure tubes are full and submerged when boiling. Drying and polishing finishes the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning new graduated pipettes
rubrics_metrics.description: Place pipettes in receptacle filled with soapy water; boil vigorously for twenty minutes over a Bunsen flame; rinse in running water and drain; run distilled water, then rectified spirits through pipettes; dry either in hot-air oven (raise slowly to ~80°C) or by blowing air through via bellows/blowpipe until interior is dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two drying options given: hot-air oven (vide p.31) or blow through with rubber tube/foot bellows. Run rectified spirits before oven/drying to aid drying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating glassware already used (infected test-tubes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pack tubes vertically in autoclave basket (remove plugs/caps); fill tubes with water; disinfect at 120°C for twenty minutes (or boil vigorously 30–45 min if no autoclave); while still hot empty and roughly clean with stiff brush; boil with soapy water for thirty minutes; brush and rinse; immerse in 2–5% hydrochloric acid for ~15 minutes; rinse in running and distilled water; invert to drain; dry and polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If autoclave unavailable, use digester or tightly covered pan and prolonged boiling. Steps 1–9 in text must be followed for thorough disinfection; similar treatment applies to infected flasks, plates, capsules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning flasks used in media preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clean immediately after use: fill with water containing soap powder and a few crystals of potassium permanganate and boil; usually cleaned with a flask brush; if not, treat with 5% nitric acid or shake with wet cotton-wool rolled in silver sand; rinse thoroughly, dry and polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potassium permanganate aids cleaning of media residues; use acid or abrasive cotton-wool for stubborn deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning infected pipettes
rubrics_metrics.description: Plunge infected pipettes immediately into tall glass cylinders containing 2% lysol and allow them to remain for some days; remove, drain and boil in soapy water for thirty minutes; rinse thoroughly in cold water; immerse in 5% nitric acid for an hour or two; rinse again in running water; complete cleaning as described under 'new pipettes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For graduated capillary blood pipettes, consider suction-aspiration cleaning method to hasten steps from alcohol/ether onward (see separate device).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid cleansing of capillary blood pipettes using suction apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Fit a Kitasato filter flask to a Sprengel or Geryk pump; attach rubber tube to side tubulure and attach pipette to rubber tubing with point downward in beaker of distilled water; start pump to aspirate water through pipette, then flush with rectified spirit and ether; detach and dry in hot-air oven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Device materially hastens lengthy steps (from running water onward) for capillary pipettes used with blood/serum. Use a sequence: distilled water → rectified spirit → ether → dry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopical slides: cleaning new slides
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow new slides to remain in alcohol acidulated with 5% hydrochloric acid for some hours; rinse in running water, drain roughly on a towel, dry, and finally polish with a selvyt cloth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only a few slides required, rub surface with jeweler's emery paper (Hubert's 00) mounted on a hardwood block as a bench tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover-slips: specification and cleaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 19 mm squares for ordinary film preps and 38x19 mm rectangles for blood films; thickness 'No. 1' (0.15–0.22 mm) required for immersion lenses. Clean by dropping into enamelled pot with 10% chromic acid, boil gently for 20 minutes (add pipe-clay/pumice to prevent spurting); wash under running water until yellow disappears, wash in distilled water, wash in rectified spirit; transfer with heated forceps to absolute alcohol and store in stopper glass pot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After chromic acid treatment, cover-slips must not be touched by fingers. Use forceps previously heated in Bunsen flame to destroy grease. Store in absolute alcohol, stoppered tightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Used slides and cover-slips: disposal and recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Discarded slides with mounted cover-slip preparations and cover-slips used for hanging-drop mounts should be thrown into pot containing 2% lysol and kept for about a week; cover-slips mounted with Canada balsam can then be detached readily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For used slides: wash thoroughly in running water, boil in soapy water for half an hour, rinse, dry and polish. For used cover-slips: treat as new in 10% chromic acid; rub off friable dirt under water if necessary; return to fresh chromic acid and treat as new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of badly scratched or hazy glassware
rubrics_metrics.description: Immerse test-tubes, plates, capsules which are scratched/hazy or cannot be cleaned otherwise in enamelled iron bath containing water acidulated to 1% with hydrofluoric acid for ten minutes; rinse thoroughly in water, dry and polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hydrofluoric acid is used only for glass that resists other cleaning methods; handle with caution (implied by special reagent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plugging test-tubes and flasks with cotton-wool
rubrics_metrics.description: Use best absorbent cotton-wool (surgeons' wool). Tear strip ~10 cm x 2 cm for a test-tube; turn in ends and roll between thumb and fingers to form long cylinder; double at centre and insert rounded end into mouth; rotate tube and screw plug into mouth ~2.5 cm leaving similar length projecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plug must be firm and fit fairly tightly—sufficient to bear weight of glass plus medium but not so tight as to prevent easy removal by a screwing motion. For larger flasks use larger strip; method identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of sterilising agents and their appropriate uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterilisation agents include chemical reagents (disinfectants/germicides) and physical agents (heat: dry heat—naked flame, muffle furnace, hot air; moist heat—water at 56°C, 100°C, streaming steam at 100°C, superheated steam at 115–120°C) and filtration (cotton-wool, porcelain filters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antiseptics (inhibit growth) are useless for sterilisation; disinfectants/germicides destroy bacterial life and are of value pending complete sterilisation. Formaldehyde is powerful but its penetrating vapour restricts use. Avoid leaving traces of disinfectants as they may vitiate experiments. A ranked list of disinfectants given (lysol 2%, perchloride of mercury 0.1%, carbolic acid 5%, absolute alcohol, ether, chloroform, camphor, thymol, toluol, volatile oils).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency rapid sterilisation with chemical washing and gentle heat
rubrics_metrics.description: In emergency, wash tubes/flasks/pipettes in turn with distilled water, perchloride of mercury solution, alcohol, and ether, drain, and finally gently heat over gas flame to drive off ether vapour; instruments dipped in ether and ignited twice may be assumed sterile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an emergency method; chloroform or other volatile disinfectants may be added to fluids and driven off by gentle heat. Repeat dipping-lighting process twice for small instruments (ether flame).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterilisation by naked flame and ether flame (dry heat short exposures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Naked Bunsen flame is used to sterilise platinum needles (heated to redness) and may be used for small instruments, cover-glasses, pipettes, etc.; ether flame: dip small instruments in ether, remove and light adherent fluid allowing it to burn off; repeat twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very short exposure is sufficient for small metal/instrument points; for ether flame repeat twice and then assume sterility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muffle furnace sterilisation (for porcelain filter candles and destruction of morbid tissues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Roll each filter bougie in asbestos cloth, secure with copper wire, place inside muffle; raise to white heat and maintain for five minutes; allow to cool completely before removal; store wrapped in asbestos in sterile metal boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Too rapid cooling before room temperature may produce microscopic cracks that destroy efficiency. Muffle chiefly for porcelain filter candles and destruction of morbid tissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot-air oven sterilisation: temperatures, timing and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Hot air at 150°C destroys bacteria, spores, etc., in ~30 minutes; momentary exposure to 175–180°C achieves same. Use hot-air oven: arrange articles (avoid cotton-wool plugs contacting walls), prepare wire crates with asbestos padding to protect tubes, open ventilator slide to let moisture escape before heating; raise to 175°C (with staged alarms at 100°C and 175°C), extinguish gas, allow oven to cool and only open when interior recorded at 60°C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent charring of cotton-wool by avoiding contact with walls. Neglecting to cool to 60°C before opening will cause many cracked/broken tubes. Metal instruments can be sterilised but exposure to 175°C blunts steel; for surgical instruments heat to 130°C for ~30 minutes packed in metal box.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractional sterilisation by moist heat at 56°C (for albuminous fluids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain water-bath at 56°C for 30 minutes to destroy vegetative bacteria (not spores); immerse tubes/flasks so fluid level is ≥2 cm below water level; cool rapidly; repeat exposure on each of six successive days to ensure thorough sterilisation (fractional sterilisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vegetative forms killed; spores may germinate between exposures and be destroyed on subsequent days. Procedure described as fractional sterilisation—30 minutes at 56°C repeated on six successive days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling water sterilisation at 100°C for instruments and small apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Water at 100°C destroys vegetative forms almost instantaneously and spores in 5–15 minutes. Use a water steriliser (rectangular copper box with wire basket). Place instruments in basket, pour water, boil until steam issues for at least ten minutes, extinguish gas, open and lift basket; after contamination boil for further fifteen minutes; dry while hot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for metal instruments, syringes, rubber corks, rubber and glass tubing, and small apparatus. After disinfection, dry immediately and return to store cases to avoid recontamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streaming steam sterilisation (Koch's/Arnold's sterilisers) and intermittent sterilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a steam steriliser: fill water compartment, allow steam to replace air (continuous stream observed), lower basket into sterilising compartment, replace lid; for fluid media allow 20 minutes, for solid media 30 minutes; remove basket only after interval and extinguish gas; repeat process after 24 hours and again for assurance (discontinuous/intermittent sterilisation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streaming steam at 100°C destroys vegetative forms in 15–20 minutes and spores in 1–2 hours but intermittent method (20 minutes on each of three successive days) recommended. Continuous sterilisation (1–2 hours) cannot always be depended upon and is not recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superheated steam (autoclave) sterilisation parameters and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Autoclave (Chamberland)—pack articles in wire basket; fill boiler water to bottom of basket and fill contained flasks/tubes with water; ensure rubber washer in place and fasten lid; open vent cock and light burners; when steady steam issues shut vent and extinguish outer burners; wait until manometer/index records 120°C, then maintain for twenty minutes; extinguish gas, allow manometer to fall to zero, open vent cock slowly to equalise, then remove contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superheated steam at 115–120°C under pressure destroys vegetative and sporing forms rapidly (115°C ~15 min; 120°C ~10 min). Higher temperatures may hydrolyse media—restrict autoclave use for contaminated articles/old cultivations. Regulate safety valve to maintain required temperature; open vent slowly when finished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sterilisation timing device usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric signal timing clock described: face surrounded by metal plate with 60 holes corresponding to minutes, each hole has a rod contacting hour hand; keyboard with numbered plugs completes circuit when hour hand touches rod, actuating alarm; used for electrically noting periods from one minute up to one hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Device useful for timing sterilisation periods and many laboratory operations. The friction contact rings for ~20 seconds giving audible signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtration for sterilising gases using dry cotton-wool filters
rubrics_metrics.description: Sterilise gases before admission by passing through a glass tube bulb filled with dry cotton-wool and wrapped cotton-wool at ends secured with wire (sterilise the assembled tube in hot-air oven); couple sterile rubber tubing from gas reservoir through filter to inlet tube of cultivation flask whose inlet is enveloped in cotton-wool; gas passing through dry sterile cotton-wool enters flask sterile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the cotton-wool remains dry—if it becomes moist mould threads penetrate and contaminate. Sterile connections: disinfect and boil rubber tubing then pass through alcohol and flame to remove traces before coupling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtration of liquids through porcelain (Chamberland/Berkefeld) filter candles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use porous biscuit porcelain (Chamberland) or kieselguhr (Berkefeld) bougie/candle fitted into stopper of filter flask; apparatus: separatory funnel, sterile filter candle with perforated rubber stopper, sterile filter flask plugged with cotton-wool, suction pump (Sprengel/Geryk or water injector), air filter sterilised, pressure tubing, screw clamps; assemble, exhaust air from filter flask, maintain vacuum and allow filtration by aspiration until complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chamberland candles have finer channels and filter more slowly than Berkefeld; Doulton white porcelain noted as efficient. Avoid candles with metal fittings (crack at junctions during sterilisation). Use aspiration or pressure to hasten slow filtration; interpose Wulff's bottle with sulphuric acid between filter flask and pump if oil-sealed pump used to protect pump oil from moisture.
